speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome to Git Going with GitHub, episode 44: Choose Your Tools. I am Alex. Today we are going to make Choose Your Tools something you can explain, practice, and recover from when the interface surprises you.

text: And I am Jamie. I will be the voice of the learner who is willing to ask, what is this for, where am I, and how do I know I did it right?

text: The big idea today: A guided tour of browser GitHub, github.dev, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, and the CLI. We will name the concept, explain why it matters, practice the move, and point out the checks that tell you the work is real.

speaker: ALEX
text: 1. Why This Matters: There is no single "right" way to use GitHub. Some switch between all of them depending on the task.

speaker: ALEX
text: The following table summarizes all five environments at a glance. Read through the summaries first, then explore the sections that interest you.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What stays the same when the tool changes?

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub.com (Browser): what it is: The GitHub website at github.com. Every repository, issue, pull request, and setting lives here.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right.

speaker: ALEX
text: What you can do here.

speaker: ALEX
text: For a learner, the useful signals are concrete. Browse repositories, files, and folders. Create, comment on, and close issues. Open, review, and merge pull requests. Edit individual files using the built-in web editor (pencil icon). Manage labels, milestones, and project boards. Configure repository settings and branch protection.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What would you say to someone who is already bracing for this to be too much?

speaker: ALEX
text: What you cannot do here.

speaker: ALEX
text: Run code or tests locally. Use a full-featured code editor with extensions. Make offline changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: That pause between action and trust is part of the work.

speaker: ALEX
text: That matters because of the next idea. Do not treat Screen reader experience as decoration. GitHub.com has strong screen reader support. Every page uses ARIA landmarks, headings follow a consistent hierarchy, and keyboard shortcuts are available for most actions.

speaker: ALEX
text: A solid navigation habit is to prove where you are before activating controls. Headings, landmarks, and the address bar are not trivia; they are your map.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How would you walk the room through that step by step?

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub supports light and dark themes, high contrast themes, and responds to your operating system's contrast preferences. GitHub's layout adapts to browser zoom up to 400% without horizontal scrolling on most pages.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start here: Go to github.com/settings/appearance. Then: Choose from Light, Dark, Light high contrast, or Dark high contrast. Next: Or select "Sync with system" to follow your OS setting. The sequence works because every action has a confirmation.

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning Cards: GitHub.com (Browser).

speaker: ALEX
text: Press S on any GitHub page to jump to the main search field; press / as an alternative. Press D in Browse Mode to jump between ARIA landmark regions; the repository tabs (Code, Issues, Pull Requests) are inside the "Repository navigation" landmark. Press G then I (two keystrokes in sequence) to jump directly to the Issues tab from anywhere in a repository. Switch to "High contrast dark" or "High contrast light" at github.com/settings/appearance for maximum border and text contrast. Browser zoom up to 200% keeps GitHub's layout intact; above 200% the repository sidebar collapses into a hamburger menu. Enable "Link underlines" in GitHub Accessibility settings so links are distinguishable without color.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is the common workflow underneath the different interfaces?

speaker: ALEX
text: What it is: A VS Code editor that runs entirely in your browser. Open any repository by pressing the.

speaker: ALEX
text: That becomes easier when you listen for these cues. Edit multiple files in a VS Code-like interface with a file explorer, tabs, and an integrated terminal preview. View file diffs and stage changes. Commit directly to a branch. Use many VS Code extensions that run in the browser.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Give me the version that sounds like an instructor, not a manual.

speaker: ALEX
text: If someone is taking notes, this is the short list. Run code, build projects, or execute terminal commands (the terminal is read-only for Git operations). Use extensions that require a local runtime (debuggers, compiled tools). Work offline.

speaker: ALEX
text: github.dev is VS Code running in the browser, so the same keyboard navigation and screen reader support applies. The command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) is available, and all editor keybindings work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I am listening before the workshop starts, what should settle in my mind first?

speaker: ALEX
text: use github.dev when you need to edit more than one file in a single commit, or when you want the code editor experience without installing anything. For single-file edits, the pencil icon on GitHub.com is simpler.

text: Yes. The named thing - the heading, tab, field, branch, or button - is the handhold.

speaker: ALEX
text: Path 3: VS Code (Desktop). What it is: Visual Studio Code is a free desktop code editor from Microsoft. This is the part to say slowly: It has built-in Git support, an integrated terminal, thousands of extensions, and GitHub Copilot included. The durable skill is not memorizing one screen. It is knowing how to find your footing when the screen changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: What you can do here.

speaker: ALEX
text: The useful version is not abstract; it sounds like this. Edit files with full IntelliSense, syntax highlighting, and extension support. Use the integrated terminal to run Git commands, scripts, and programs. Stage, commit, push, and pull using the Source Control panel or the terminal. Run and debug code. Use GitHub Copilot for code suggestions, chat, and code review. Work offline (Git operations sync when you reconnect).

speaker: ALEX
text: The next point gives the learner a handle. What you cannot do here (without extensions).

speaker: ALEX
text: This is where the lesson becomes something you can check. Manage GitHub issues and pull requests directly (install the GitHub Pull Requests extension for this). View repository insights or settings (use GitHub.com for that).

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where do you want a learner to place their attention here?

speaker: ALEX
text: VS Code has a dedicated accessibility mode that activates automatically when a screen reader is detected. Deep dive: Chapter 11 covers the VS Code interface in detail.

speaker: ALEX
text: A few details make that real. Screen reader optimized mode announces line content, cursor position, and editor state. The Accessibility Help dialog (Alt+F1 or Option+F1) is available in every view. All panels are reachable via keyboard shortcuts.

speaker: ALEX
text: Hold that next to this. Put Low vision experience into plain language. VS Code supports high contrast themes, custom zoom levels (Ctrl+= to zoom in, Ctrl+- to zoom out), and configurable font sizes. The useful version is: The minimap (the small code preview on the right side of the editor) can be disabled if it is distracting: open the command palette, type "minimap," and toggle the setting. The interface gets easier when it becomes a set of named places instead of a wall of controls.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the learner is not behind if they stop there and check the page.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Pausing to verify is not a detour; it is how you keep control of the workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: There are a lot of tools in play. How do we keep that from feeling like a contest?

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning Cards: VS Code (Desktop).

speaker: ALEX
text: Press Ctrl+Shift+E to focus the File Explorer tree; Up/Down Arrow navigates files, Enter opens a file, Right Arrow expands a folder. Press Ctrl+Shift+G to focus Source Control; the tree lists changed files and each item announces its Git status (modified, untracked, etc.). Press Alt+F1 inside any view to open the Accessibility Help dialog, which lists every keyboard shortcut for that specific panel. Press Ctrl+K Ctrl+T to open the theme picker; "High Contrast" and "High Contrast Light" offer the strongest visual differentiation. Press Ctrl+= repeatedly to zoom the entire interface; the zoom level persists after restart. Disable the minimap to reclaim screen width: Ctrl+Shift+P, type "minimap", toggle "Editor: Minimap Enabled" off.

speaker: ALEX
text: That connects to another useful point. What it is: A desktop application that provides a graphical interface for Git operations. Instead of typing git commit in a terminal, you use buttons, lists, and visual diffs.

text: On the ground, that means a few things. Clone repositories with one click. Create, switch, and merge branches. View file diffs in a side-by-side or unified view. Stage individual files or specific lines within a file. Commit with a message and push to GitHub. Open pull requests (launches GitHub.com).

speaker: ALEX
text: Here is the practical turn. What you cannot do here.

speaker: ALEX
text: Edit code (GitHub Desktop is a Git client, not a code editor -- it opens your preferred editor). Review pull requests with inline comments. Manage issues, labels, or project boards.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Screen reader experience. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub Desktop uses Electron and provides basic screen reader support. Branch switching, commit history, and file lists are navigable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is a useful checkpoint before anyone starts pressing keys.

speaker: ALEX

speaker: ALEX
text: Keep the thread going. Choose GitHub Desktop if you prefer a visual representation of branches and commits, and you do not want to memorize Git commands. This is the part to say slowly: It is a good stepping stone between the GitHub.com web editor and the full VS Code workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on 7. Path 5: GitHub CLI. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: What it is: A command-line tool called gh that brings GitHub features to your terminal. It handles authentication, issue management, pull request workflows, and repository operations -- directly from the command line.

speaker: ALEX
text: Another way to ground it. What you can do here.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here is the part that makes the next action easier. Create, view, and close issues: gh issue create, gh issue view 42. Open, review, merge PRs: gh pr create, gh pr review, gh pr merge. Clone repos and manage branches: gh repo clone owner/repo. View CI/CD status: gh run list, gh run view. Manage repository settings, labels, and releases. Automate workflows with shell scripts.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on What you cannot do here. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: These are the pieces that turn the idea into a usable move. Edit files (the CLI manages GitHub operations, not file editing -- use your preferred editor). View visual diffs (use git diff for text-based diffs, or VS Code for a richer view).

speaker: ALEX
text: This is the part worth saying out loud. Put Screen reader experience into plain language. The GitHub CLI is a text-based tool running in a terminal. The useful version is: Screen reader users read its output directly as plain text -- no landmarks, headings, or ARIA to worry about.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I like that because it gives people permission to slow down.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the goal. We want the page to feel explorable, not fragile.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on When to choose GitHub CLI. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: Choose the CLI if you are comfortable in a terminal and want fast, scriptable access to GitHub features. It pairs well with VS Code's integrated terminal, giving you the best of both worlds.

speaker: ALEX
text: Put that beside the next piece. Learning Cards: GitHub CLI.

speaker: ALEX
text: Listen for the small confirmations in this list. CLI output is plain text; use Up Arrow to re-read previous lines or pipe output through more to page through long results. Run gh issue list --state open and output reads as a tab-separated table; each row is one line your screen reader can navigate. Use gh pr view --web to open the current PR directly in your browser where full ARIA landmarks are available. Increase terminal font size in VS Code: Settings (Ctrl+,), search "terminal.integrated.fontSize" and set to 18-24. Use gh pr diff to view diffs in the terminal with colored additions (green) and deletions (red); if colors are hard to see, pipe through less -R for paginated output. Set your terminal theme to high contrast in VS Code's theme picker (Ctrl+K Ctrl+T) to improve command and output readability.

text: 8. Which Path Should I Start With?: There is no wrong answer, but here is practical guidance based on when different tools become most useful in the workshop.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now shift from knowing the term to using it. On Day 2, you work with Git locally. Most students add VS Code (Path 3) at this point.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Switching paths is normal. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: the learner will likely use more than one tool during the workshop. The workshop chapters always tell you which tool to use for each step.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here are the anchors worth keeping. Browse the repository on GitHub.com to understand its structure. Edit files in VS Code or github.dev for a better coding experience. Manage branches in GitHub Desktop if you prefer the visual workflow. Automate repetitive tasks with the GitHub CLI.

speaker: ALEX

speaker: ALEX
text: These are the details that keep the idea from floating away. Start with GitHub.com on Day 1; its ARIA landmarks, heading hierarchy, and single-key shortcuts (G I for Issues, G P for Pull Requests) provide the most navigable experience. When Day 2 adds VS Code, press Shift+Alt+F1 immediately to enable Screen Reader Optimized mode before doing anything else. You can switch tools mid-exercise; the workshop always tells you which tool each step targets, so look for the tool name at the start of each instruction. GitHub.com at 150-200% zoom with a high-contrast theme is the easiest starting environment; no installation needed. When you add VS Code on Day 2, set both the editor zoom (Ctrl+=) and the font size (Settings, "editor.fontSize") independently for maximum comfort. GitHub Desktop's visual branch diagram uses thin colored lines; if those are hard to see, stick with VS Code's Source Control panel which uses text labels.

text: This exercise takes approximately five minutes. It verifies your tool is working and builds your confidence before Day 1 begins.
